This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings from a post-election survey conducted November 10-14, 2016, on voter opinions of the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The main text highlights that while half of voters were happy with Donald Trump's victory, his campaign conduct received the lowest approval ratings for any winning candidate in 28 years, with only 30% giving him an A or B grade. The central visual element is a line chart comparing the percentage of voters who gave "A" or "B" grades to winning and losing candidates across eight elections from 1988 to 2016, showing a significant drop in approval for Trump compared to previous winners like Obama (75%) and Bush (75%). The data reveals a stark contrast between public satisfaction with the outcome and the negative evaluation of the campaign process.

This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings from a post-election survey conducted November 10-14, 2016, on voter opinions of the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The main text highlights that while half of voters were happy with Donald Trump's victory, his campaign conduct received the lowest approval ratings for any winning candidate in 28 years, with only 30% giving him an A or B grade. The central visual element is a line chart comparing the percentage of voters who gave "A" or "B" grades to winning and losing candidates across eight elections from 1988 to 2016, showing a significant drop in approval for Trump compared to previous winners like Obama (75%) and Bush (75%). The data reveals a stark contrast between public satisfaction with the outcome and the negative evaluation of the campaign process.

**Text Evidence:**
- The survey was conducted by Pew Research Center from November 10-14, 2016, among 1,254 voters.
- 50% of voters are happy that Trump won; 48% are unhappy.
- Just 30% of voters give Trump an A or B grade for his campaign conduct.
- 35% of voters give Trump a failing grade (D or F).
- In 2008, 75% of voters gave Barack Obama an A or B grade.
- Voters' evaluations of the campaign are more negative than after any election since 1988.

The highest grade for a winning candidate was 75% for Obama in 2008, while the lowest was 30% for Trump in 2016.</chart_summary>

Grading the 2016 election Donald Trump receives low grades for how he conducted himself over the course of the campaign, but voters grade other campaign actors just as harshly and in some cases even more harshly. Only about a quarter give an A or B to the Republican Party (22%) and the Democratic Party (26%). About three-in-ten give the parties an F (30% for Republican Party, 28% Democratic Party), by far the highest share giving the parties failing grades since this series of surveys began in 1988. Voters also give abysmal grades to the press and pollsters, whose pre-election surveys were widely criticized. Just  $22\%$  give the press a grade of an A or B, while  $38\%$  give it a failing grade. Similarly, fewer voters award pollsters grades of A or B  $(21\%)$  than a grade of F  $(30\%)$ . And voters do not spare themselves from criticism. Just  $40\%$  give "the voters" a grade of A or B – the lowest percentage after any election since 1996. As our surveys found throughout the campaign, voters view the 2016 contest as extraordinarily negative. Fully  $92 \%$ say there was more “mudslinging” or negative campaigning than in past elections – which is 20 percentage points higher than the previous high (72% after the 2004 election). And while a large majority of voters  $(81\%)$  feel they learned enough about the candidates to make an informed choice, a record  $73\%$  say that there was less discussion of issues compared with past presidential campaigns. This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings from a voter callback survey conducted November 10-14, 2016, on public perceptions of the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The main content includes a table titled "Election report card: Barely passing grades" which provides overall grades for key campaign actors like Donald Trump, Hillary Clinton, the Republican and Democratic parties, the press, pollsters, and voters themselves. A line chart illustrates the record-high percentage of voters who felt there was more mudslinging in the 2016 campaign compared to past elections. The text highlights that voters gave low grades across the board, with over 30% giving failing grades to the major parties, the press, and pollsters, and notes that the 92% figure for increased mudslinging is the highest recorded since 1988.

**Text Evidence:**
- Donald Trump received a C- average grade, while Hillary Clinton received a C.
- Only 22% of voters gave the Republican Party an A or B, and 26% gave the Democratic Party an A or B.
- 30% of voters gave the Republican Party an F, and 28% gave the Democratic Party an F.
- Just 22% of voters gave the press an A or B, and 38% gave it an F.
- 21% of voters gave pollsters an A or B, and 30% gave them an F.
- 40% of voters gave "the voters" an A or B, the lowest percentage after any election since 1996.
- 92% of voters said there was more "mudslinging" or negative campaigning than in past elections, a record high.
- 73% of voters said there was less discussion of issues compared with past campaigns.

elements.text: Grading the 2016 election

Donald Trump receives low grades for how he conducted himself over the course of the campaign, but voters grade other campaign actors just as harshly and in some cases even more harshly. Only about a quarter give an A or B to the Republican Party (22%) and the Democratic Party (26%). About three-in-ten give the parties an F (30% for Republican Party, 28% Democratic Party), by far the highest share giving the parties failing grades since this series of surveys began in 1988.

Voters also give abysmal grades to the press and pollsters, whose pre-election surveys were widely criticized. Just  $22\%$  give the press a grade of an A or B, while  $38\%$  give it a failing grade. Similarly, fewer voters award pollsters grades of A or B  $(21\%)$  than a grade of F  $(30\%)$ .
And voters do not spare themselves from criticism. Just  $40\%$  give "the voters" a grade of A or B – the lowest percentage after any election since 1996.

Other important findings Voters pessimistic on how Trump will impact race relations. Nearly half of voters (46%) say Trump's election will lead to worse race relations, while only about half as many (25%) expect race relations to improve; 26% say his election won't make a difference. Among Clinton voters, 84% expect race relations to worsen under Trump. Among Trump supporters, half expect improvement, while 38% say his election won't make a difference. Post-victory, most Trump backers confident in an accurate vote count. In August, just  $38\%$  of registered voters who supported Trump were very confident that their vote would be counted accurately. But in the aftermath of Trump's victory,  $75\%$  expressed confidence that their votes were counted accurately. The views of Clinton supporters showed no change: After the election  $67\%$  were confident that their votes were counted accurately. Most expect woman president, eventually. Following Clinton's defeat, a sizable majority of voters (79%) still expect there will be a female president "in their lifetime." There are no significant differences in these opinions among men and women, or Clinton supporters and Trump backers. Voters say press has too much influence. Voters grade the press very negatively, and most (57%) say it had too much influence on the outcome of the election. Just  $27 \%$ say the PEW RESEARCH CENTER press had the right amount of influence on the election, while  $13\%$  say it had too little influence. About six-in-ten Trump voters  $(62\%)$  say the press had too much influence, as do  $50\%$  of Clinton voters.

This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings on voter confidence in Donald Trump across five major issues, based on a survey conducted from November 10-14, 2016. The main text and a bar chart show that voters have the highest confidence in Trump regarding the economy (62% have at least a fair amount of confidence) and the threat of terrorism (56%). Confidence is more divided on health care, illegal immigration, and foreign policy, with roughly half of voters expressing little or no confidence in each area. The data is presented as percentages for different levels of confidence: "a great deal," "a fair amount," "not too much," and "none at all."

- 56% of voters have at least a fair amount of confidence in Trump regarding the threat of terrorism.

At least nine-in-ten Trump voters say they have at least a fair amount of confidence in him on each of these five issues. However, the share expressing a great deal of confidence in Trump varies by issue. Seven-in-ten of his voters have a great deal of confidence that he will do the right thing on the economy (70%), and nearly as many (64%) say this about the threat of terrorism. Yet fewer express a great deal of confidence that he will do the right thing when it comes to health care (58%) or illegal immigration (55%), and only about half (47%) of Trump voters express a great deal of confidence in him on foreign policy. Conversely, most Clinton voters say they have not too much or no confidence at all that Trump will do the right thing on all of these issues. On four of five issues, over  $80\%$  of Clinton supporters say they have not too much or no confidence. Nearly two-thirds of Clinton supporters say they have no confidence at all in Trump to do the right thing when it comes to illegal immigration  $(64\%)$  or foreign policy  $(63\%)$ . However, just  $40\%$  say they have no confidence in Trump when it comes to dealing with the economy. This page from a Pew Research Center report presents data on confidence levels in Donald Trump among his supporters and Clinton voters across five key issues: economy, threat of terrorism, health care, illegal immigration, and foreign policy. The main content consists of two stacked bar charts (Figures) showing the percentage of voters who have "a great deal," "a fair amount," "not too much," or "none at all" confidence in Trump to do the right thing on each issue. The text explains that while most Trump voters express at least a fair amount of confidence, the level of "great deal" confidence varies significantly by issue, with the highest support for the economy (70%) and lowest for foreign policy (47%). In contrast, Clinton voters overwhelmingly lack confidence, with over 80% expressing "not too much" or "no confidence" on four of the five issues. The data reveals a stark partisan divide but also shows that both groups rate Trump similarly relative to each other on the same issues.

**Text Evidence:**
- At least nine-in-ten Trump voters say they have at least a fair amount of confidence in him on each of the five issues.
- 70% of Trump voters have a great deal of confidence he will do the right thing on the economy.
- 64% of Trump voters have a great deal of confidence on the threat of terrorism.
- 58% of Trump voters have a great deal of confidence on health care.
- 55% of Trump voters have a great deal of confidence on illegal immigration.
- 47% of Trump voters have a great deal of confidence on foreign policy.
- Over 80% of Clinton voters say they have not too much or no confidence on four of the five issues.
- 64% of Clinton voters have no confidence at all in Trump on illegal immigration.
- 63% of Clinton voters have no confidence at all in Trump on foreign policy.
- 27% of Clinton supporters say they have at least a fair amount of confidence in Trump on the economy.
- 99% of Trump supporters say they have at least a fair amount of confidence in Trump on the economy.

<figure_summary>Figure: Among Clinton voters - Stacked bar chart showing the percentage of Clinton voters who have confidence in Donald Trump to do the right thing when dealing with five issues. SECTION: Low Marks for Major Players in 2016 Election - Including the Winner - 2. Prospects for bipartisan cooperation, ideological direction of the parties (Pages 23-28)

TOPICS: public opinion on bipartisan cooperation, partisan relations, voter attitudes toward Trump and Clinton, party ideological direction, voter evaluations of campaign participants, survey data from Pew Research Center

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 79% of Americans said the country is more politically divided than in the past (Page 23)
- In 2016, 27% of voters think relations between Republicans and Democrats will improve, 27% expect them to worsen, and 45% expect them to stay the same (Page 23)
- 47% of Trump voters expect relations to improve, while only 10% of Clinton voters expect improvement (Page 23)
- 9% of Trump voters expect relations to get worse, while 43% of Clinton voters expect worsening (Page 23)
- In 2008, 37% of voters expected relations to get better, 18% expected them to get worse, and 42% expected little change (Page 23)
- 55% of Obama voters in 2008 expected improvements, compared to 47% of Trump voters in 2016 (Page 23)
- 43% of Clinton voters today expect relations to worsen, compared to 31% of McCain voters in 2008 (Page 23)
- 73% of all voters say Donald Trump should try to work with Democratic leaders to accomplish things, even if it disappoints some Republican supporters (Page 24)
- 55% of Trump voters and 90% of Clinton voters support Trump working with Democrats (Page 24)
- 37% of Trump voters believe Trump should stand up to Democrats on important issues (Page 24)
- In 2012, 56% of Obama voters and 90% of Romney backers wanted cooperation (Page 24)
- In 2008, 78% of Obama's voters and 76% of McCain's voters supported Democratic leaders working with Republicans (Page 24)
- 59% of voters say Democratic leaders should work with Trump even if it means disappointing some Democrats (Page 25)
- 39% of voters want Democrats to "stand up" to Trump, even if it means less is accomplished (Page 25)
- 83% of Trump voters say Democratic leaders should work with Trump to get things done (Page 25)
- 35% of Clinton voters hold this view, while 63% of Clinton voters say Democrats should stand up to Trump (Page 25)
- Among Clinton voters willing to give Trump a chance (58%), 51% still want Democrats to stand up to him (Page 25)
- Among Clinton voters who can't give Trump a chance (39%), 78% want Democrats to stand up to him (Page 25)
- In 2008, 58% of McCain voters said Republican leaders should try to work with Obama (Page 25)
- 60% of Republican/Rep-leaning voters want the GOP to move in a more conservative direction, compared to 36% who want more moderation (Page 26)
- 49% of Democratic/Dem-leaning voters want their party to move in a more liberal direction, while 47% prefer more moderation (Page 26)
- The share of Democrats wanting a more liberal stance has increased significantly from 38% in 2014 (Page 26)
- Data from 2008, 2012, and 2016 is based on voters; data from 2010 and 2014 is based on registered voters (Page 26)
- About half (52%) of voters say they are happy that the Republican Party maintained control of the U.S. Congress (Page 27)
- 45% of voters say they are unhappy with the GOP retaining congressional control (Page 27)
- 94% of Trump supporters are happy with the result (Page 27)
- 87% of Clinton supporters are unhappy with the result (Page 27)
- Voters gave Donald Trump an average grade of C-; 30% gave him an A or B, 19% a C, 15% a D, and 35% an F (Page 28)
- Hillary Clinton received an average grade of C; 43% gave her an A or B, 20% a C, 16% a D, and 21% an F (Page 28)
- This is the first time a losing candidate has received more positive grades than the winner (Page 28)
- The Republican Party received a D+ average (22% A/B, 25% C, 22% D, 30% F), and the Democratic Party received a C- (26% A/B, 26% C, 20% D, 28% F) (Page 28)
- The press received a failing grade from 38% of voters (22% A/B, 19% C, 21% D, 38% F) (Page 28)
- Pollsters received a failing grade from 30% of voters (21% A/B, 24% C, 21% D, 30% F) (Page 28)

- Voters gave Donald Trump an average grade of C-; 30% gave him an A or B, 19% a C, 15% a D, and 35% an F (Page 28)

- Pollsters received a failing grade from 30% of voters (21% A/B, 24% C, 21% D, 30% F) (Page 28)

- Trump receives historically low grades overall (30% A or B) (Page 29)

This page presents voter evaluations of the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, showing that voters awarded low grades to all major participants, including candidates Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, political parties, the press, and pollsters. The data, from a Pew Research Center survey conducted November 10-14, 2016, is presented in a stacked bar chart titled "Voters grade the parties, press and pollsters quite negatively," which visually compares the percentage of voters giving A or B, C, D, or F grades for each entity. Key findings include that Clinton received more positive grades than Trump, marking the first time a losing candidate outperformed the winner, while both parties, the press, and pollsters were viewed very negatively.

**Text Evidence:**
- Voters gave Donald Trump an average grade of C-; 30% gave him an A or B, 19% a C, 15% a D, and 35% an F.
- Hillary Clinton received an average grade of C; 43% gave her an A or B, 20% a C, 16% a D, and 21% an F.
- This is the first time a losing candidate has received more positive grades than the winner.
- The Republican Party received a D+ average (22% A/B, 25% C, 22% D, 30% F), and the Democratic Party received a C- (26% A/B, 26% C, 20% D, 28% F).
- The press received a failing grade from 38% of voters (22% A/B, 19% C, 21% D, 38% F).
- Pollsters received a failing grade from 30% of voters (21% A/B, 24% C, 21% D, 30% F).

The main content includes two stacked bar charts showing the percentage of voters who gave each candidate a grade of A or B, C, D, or F for their campaign conduct. SECTION: Low Marks for Major Players in 2016 Election - Including the Winner - 4. The voting process (Pages 40-44)

TOPICS: voter confidence, voting methods, wait times, decision timing, survey methodology

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Overall voter confidence in the accuracy of vote counting increased significantly after the 2016 election, particularly among Trump supporters (Page 40)
- In August 2016, 28% of registered voters were very confident and 34% were somewhat confident about an accurate national vote count; by November, 82% of those who voted said they were confident (Page 40)
- Among Trump voters, 51% were not too or not at all confident in August 2016, which dropped to 11% by November 2016 (Page 40)
- Among Clinton voters, 79% were very or somewhat confident in August 2016, decreasing slightly to 76% in November 2016 (Page 40)
- 75% of Trump voters now say they are "very" confident their own vote was counted accurately—double the share from August (Page 41)
- 67% of Clinton voters now say they are very confident their vote was counted accurately, identical to their August level (Page 41)
- 59% of voters cast their ballot on Election Day; 41% voted early (Page 42)
- In 2004, only 20% of voters said they voted before Election Day (Page 42)
- Trump voters: 39% voted early; Clinton voters: 42% voted early (Page 42)
- 39% of in-person voters reported having to wait in line; 61% did not (Page 42)
- 23% of all voters waited less than 30 minutes; 15% waited longer (Page 42)
- 48% of early in-person voters had to wait in line; 22% waited longer than 30 minutes (Page 42)
- 35% of Election Day voters had to wait; 13% waited longer than 30 minutes (Page 42)
- Overall, 20% of voters say they made up their minds about who they were voting for before 2016 (Page 43)
- About half of voters say they decided early in the year (22%) or during and just after the party conventions (32%) (Page 43)
- 15% say they definitely decided to vote for their candidate during or just after the debates (Page 43)
- 7% decided within a week of Election Day (Page 43)
- Voters' reports of when they made their decision vary little between Trump and Clinton voters (Page 43)
- The survey was conducted among 1,254 voters from November 10-14, 2016 (Page 44)
- The sample consists of registered voters aged 18 or older who were previously interviewed in Pew Research surveys from August 9-16, 2016 (n=1,567) and October 20-25, 2016 (n=2,120) (Page 44)
- Interviews were conducted on both landline telephones (312 respondents) and cell phones (942 respondents) (Page 44)
- Weighting was performed in two stages: a first-stage weight from the original datasets and a second-stage raking to match demographics including sex, age, education, region, race/ethnicity, population density, and phone use (Page 44)
- A parameter was added to the weighting so that the survey's reported vote results match the actual popular vote results (Page 44)

The text explains that overall confidence increased significantly, particularly among Trump supporters, who showed a dramatic shift from low to high confidence. pages.ocr_text: Methodology The analysis in this report is based on telephone interviews conducted November 10-14, 2016 among a national sample of 1,254 voters ("Voters" are those who said they voted in the 2016 election). The interviews were conducted among registered voters, 18 years of age or older previously interviewed in one of two Pew Research survey conducted of 1,567 registered voters in August 9-16, 2016 and 2,120 registered voters in October 20-25, 2016 (for more on the methodologies of the original surveys, see here and here). The survey was conducted by interviewers at Princeton Data Source under the direction of Princeton Survey Research Associates International. Interviews were conducted on both landline telephones and cell phones (312 respondents for this survey were interviewed on a landline telephone, and 942 were interviewed on a cell phone). Interviews were conducted in English and Spanish. Interviewers asked to speak with the respondent from the previous interview by first name, if it was available, or by age and gender. For detailed information about our survey methodology, see http://www.pewresearch.org/methodology/u-s-survey-research/ Weighting was performed in two stages. The weight from the original sample datasets was used as a first-stage weight for this project. This first-stage weight corrects for different probabilities of selection and differential non-response associated with the original interview. The sample of all registered voters contacted for this survey was then raked - by form - to match parameters for sex by age, sex by education, age by education, region, race/ethnicity, population density, phone use. The non-Hispanic, white subgroup was also raked to age, education and region. These parameters came from the weighted demographics of registered voters interviewed from the original surveys from which sample was drawn. In addition, a parameter was added to the weighting so that the vote results reported in the survey match the actual popular vote results. Sampling errors and statistical tests of significance take into account the effect of weighting.

pages.summary:
This page from the Pew Research Center presents a table detailing the unweighted sample sizes and sampling errors for various subgroups in a survey conducted from November 10-14, 2016. The table provides data on the total sample, Trump voters, Clinton voters, Republican/Lean Rep, and Democrat/Lean Dem, including their weighted proportions, unweighted sample sizes, and margin of error at the 95% confidence level. The page also includes textual information about potential sources of error beyond sampling, such as question wording and practical difficulties, and notes that the Pew Research Center operates in compliance with the Telephone Consumer Protection Act and is a nonprofit subsidiary of The Pew Charitable Trusts.

- The survey was conducted from November 10-14, 2016.
- The total unweighted sample size was 1,254.
- The margin of error for the total sample is 3.4 percentage points.
